opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's honestly one of those moments where you step back and realize how fast things are moving. If you'd asked people even a year or two before whether a model would get gold at the IMO, natural language end to end, no special formal-proof system bolted on, a lot of folks would have said that's still pretty far out. And then it just happened.

For me, the interesting part isn't only "we hit gold." It's *how* we got there. It wasn't some bespoke, narrow system built only for olympiad geometry. It was much closer to a general model that's been trained to think longer, explore, check its own work, and stay coherent over a long chain of reasoning. That says the recipe generalizes. The same ingredients that make a model better at hard math also make it better at coding, at research-style problems, at anything where you have to grind through many steps without falling apart.

On pace, I think people underestimate how compounding this is. Every capability jump feeds back into the next one. Better reasoning models help you generate better data, evaluate better, debug training runs faster. So the curve doesn't feel linear from the inside. It feels like the ground keeps shifting under you.

That said, I'd add a bit of nuance. IMO problems are hard, but they're well-posed. There's a clean answer and a clear notion of a correct proof. The real world is messier: ambiguous goals, no verifier, long horizons. So I see IMO gold less as "we're done" and more as a really strong signal that reasoning is no longer the bottleneck people thought it was. The frontier now moves to things like open-ended research, reliability, and taking long sequences of actions in the real world.

But yeah, as a researcher it's a very fun time. Things that felt like five-year problems are turning into one-year problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the IMO gold thing is interesting, but maybe not for the reason people assume. A lot of folks look at it and go, "oh wow, AI can do olympiad math now, we're basically at AGI." And I think that's a bit of a leap. What it actually tells me is more about how much the field has shifted in the last couple of years toward test-time compute and reasoning-style training. Like, if you'd asked me three years ago whether a general model would get IMO gold with natural language proofs, I'd have said sure, eventually, but I would have guessed it would need a lot more formal verification scaffolding, Lean, that kind of thing. The fact that it came out of a general model with RL on reasoning is the surprising part to me.

The other thing I'd say is that the pace feels fast, but it's also kind of uneven. Math is a domain where you have a very clean signal, right? There's a correct answer, you can verify it, you can generate tons of problems. So it's almost the ideal environment for the current recipe. I'm much less sure how well that translates to messy real-world tasks where there's no verifier and the reward is ambiguous. So I wouldn't extrapolate linearly from "IMO gold" to "solves everything."

And honestly, as someone who's been inside these labs, I'd also say a lot of what looks like a sudden jump from the outside is actually pretty incremental on the inside. It's a lot of boring work on data, infra, RL stability, eval hygiene, and then at some point it crosses a threshold and it looks like magic. So the signal I take from it is less "the curve is going vertical" and more "the recipe is working and people have figured out how to scale it." Which is still a big deal, it's just a different story than the one that usually gets told.

astra-6.text:
I think it shows how quickly the frontier is moving. Problems that we thought would remain difficult for a long time are becoming tractable much sooner than expected. And it’s not just about knowing more facts—these are problems where you have to find an approach, work through it, and produce a coherent proof.

But I’d distinguish that from being able to do original mathematical research reliably. A competition gives you a well-defined problem that you know has a solution. Research is much messier: you have to decide what questions are worth asking. So this is a really exciting milestone, and it should update our expectations about the pace of progress, but there’s still a meaningful gap between solving very hard problems and autonomously choosing and pursuing new ones.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it tells us that the frontier is moving incredibly fast, especially in reasoning. Problems that felt like distant milestones suddenly become things a model can solve at a very high level. And then we adjust our expectations almost immediately, which is quite remarkable.

But I’d distinguish between reaching that level on a competition and having that capability reliably across everything people do. An IMO gold is a very significant milestone. It doesn’t mean every mathematical problem is solved or that research is automated. The next question is how broadly those reasoning capabilities transfer, and how reliably we can use them.
